hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
RAG vs. Graph RAG vs. Agentic RAG, clearly explained!

Standard RAG embeds documents into vectors and retrieves the most similar chunks via similarity search. For direct factual lookups, this works well.

But it breaks down when a query needs to connect facts spread across multiple documents. Similarity search retrieves individual chunks, not the relationships between them.

Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer on top.

→ During indexing, an LLM extracts entities and relationships from the documents.

→ During retrieval, the system traverses these connections instead of relying on embedding similarity alone.

This is what enables multi-hop queries.

Say a vector DB stores three facts about internal services:

↳ "The checkout service uses payments API."
↳ "The payments API runs on cluster-3."
↳ "Cluster-3 is scheduled for maintenance on Friday."

Someone asks: "Will the checkout service be affected by Friday's maintenance?"

Vector search can likely retrieve facts 1 and 3 because the query mentions "checkout service" and "Friday maintenance."

But it will miss fact 2, which connects the payments API to cluster-3.

That middle fact sits too far from the query in embedding space. It mentions neither "checkout" nor "maintenance," so it never makes it into the retrieved context.

A knowledge graph connects these as linked entities, and graph traversal finds the full path in one query.

Agentic RAG takes a different approach entirely.

Instead of a fixed retrieval pipeline, an LLM agent decides at query time which tools to invoke, which sources to query, and in what order.

Check the visual below to understand the three architectures thoroughly.

One thing to note here is that these three aren't levels of sophistication that you need to graduate through.

Instead, they solve different query types.

↳ Single-hop factual lookups → standard RAG
↳ Multi-hop relationship queries → Graph RAG
↳ Dynamic multi-source tasks with tool use → Agentic RAG

Once the right architecture is in place, the next leverage point is efficiency.

Most RAG architectures rely heavily on vector search, and that layer can be made 32x more memory-efficient using binary quantization.

I covered the full implementation in the article below.

hits.name: Thorsten Ball
hits.text:
Loose thoughts on the future of abstractions:

At first glance, it seems evident that shared abstractions (stdlibs, frameworks, libraries) will still be beneficial in a world of agents. Centralized and shared knowledge, lower costs (no tokens needed) are just two reasons for why this is good.

But, looking back at the last ten years, it's clear that a lot of frameworks and libraries were made due to (to simplify) personal preference: framework X is Y but in language Foo which has same runtime characteristics as Bar but I like it better, or framework X was born out of frustration with syntax of Y, or framework X uses TOML instead of YAML and is container-native or ... <insert favorite thing here>.

Meaning: a lot of abstractions in the last twenty years were made for reasons that no longer seem valid.

That makes me think that there will be less need for more abstractions (as we've known them!) in the future. But if you look around, you'll see that there's a thousand new things being created every day. I think that's a temporary phase.

There are other, deeper (for lack of a better term) abstractions though that still seem valid: abstractions that introduce a different way to compute. Think: type systems, Lisps, CUDA, unikernels, IaC, k8s. (That's not a final and super confident list, more a general pointing in a direction. I'm unsure here.)

I do think that in the future people will still create new abstractions of this latter type. Sharing those is still valuable, because they go along with a platform or a product.

But the former type -- different languages that just switch syntax, frameworks that fix one grievance, util-like stdlibs -- for that I can see a future in which we're just endlessly remixing and "vendoring" existing abstractions.

And just to say this out loud: I do think a lot of code-level abstractions (MVC, composition over inheritance, avoid-god-objects, classes vs. modules) don't matter in the future, because they're born out of the ability of humans to understand and maintain code.

Even if new abstractions in this realm might make sense in the future, I think the barrier for them to spread is now incredibly high.

Example: friend reported that in his company they're trying to introduce a new pattern because "adding a new country to our system requires changing all of these places in this 1500-line long class" -- who gives a shit about that anymore?

Oh and another thing: I think the "is it in the training data?" concern is way overblown by now. Intelligence generalizes to a certain degree and the latest models have 0 problems writing in a language or framework that you just made up. Try it.
